intro: A hen’s repeated clucking becomes a keyboard figure that can change harmony, register and weight. Marcelle Meyer plays Rameau’s harpsichord piece on piano, keeping the repeated attack at the centre of the argument.
question: How much can Rameau build from a repeated note?

sections.label: First strain · the repeated-note figure
sections.mNote: clucking figure grows into chords and running passages

sections.label: Second strain · the figure renewed

cues.title: A hen in notation
cues.text: Rameau writes the hen’s “co co co” beneath repeated notes at the opening. The little rising flourish attached to the repeated pitch becomes part of the musical vocabulary: listen for the difference between reiterating one note and suddenly opening out into a run.
cues.evidence: The inspected keyboard score prints the syllables beneath the opening and repeatedly combines reiteration with flourishes. This describes the written figure, not a machine-identified animal sound. Score scan, printed pp. 86–89: https://archive.org/download/imslp-suites-de-pices-de-clavecin-rameau-jean-philippe/Rameau_-_nouvelles_suite.pdf
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Character inside a suite
cues.text: La Poule belongs to the G-centred group in the Nouvelles Suites de pièces de clavecin. Dances and character pieces share the collection: the title supplies an image, while key and keyboard technique connect it to its neighbours.
cues.evidence: The score places La Poule after the menuets and before Les Triolets; the collection’s G-major/minor grouping is also described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Philippe_Rameau#Harpsichord_music

cues.title: One note acquires weight
cues.text: Across the piece, the repeated figure appears both as an exposed line and inside thicker chords. Keep hold of its rhythm when the surrounding harmony changes; a new weight of attack need not mean a new idea.
cues.evidence: Printed pp. 86–89 show the single-note figure, repeated chordal writing and fort/doux contrasts. The report’s sharp level change between 1:00 and 1:05 supports local contrast but does not identify the exact chord or a pedal technique.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Theory before the theatre
cues.text: Rameau publishes his Traité de l’harmonie in 1722, before his operatic career begins. His first opera, Hippolyte et Aricie, reaches the Paris Opéra in 1733, shortly after his fiftieth birthday.
cues.evidence: Dates and career order agree with the existing Rameau biography and the documented biography at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Philippe_Rameau#Life

cues.title: Repetition changes its surroundings
cues.text: In the second strain, familiar repeated notes coexist with decorated upper lines and changing bass support. Listen below the clucking figure: the bass can redirect the phrase even while the surface rhythm remains recognisable.
cues.evidence: The second strain begins near the end of printed p. 87 and continues on pp. 88–89. Its approximate placement after the strong 1:34 boundary is consistent with the report; the local D-minor estimates are corroboration only, not individual chord labels.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Meyer’s twentieth-century keyboard
cues.text: This is Marcelle Meyer at the piano, recorded at Salle Adyar in Paris on 29–30 October 1953 according to the source and discography. Rameau’s original instrument is the harpsichord; Meyer’s piano changes the available sustain and dynamic weight.
cues.evidence: Commons names the session and DF 98/99; Classical Pianists chronology, entry MaMe-C#015, gives the same date and venue. The 22 August 2019 Commons Date field is the upload date. https://classical-pianists.net/viii/marcelle-meyer/chronology/

cues.title: Let the last attacks settle
cues.text: Towards the close, separate repeated attacks give way to the final resonance. Keep listening after the last forceful gesture: the remaining sound is not another repetition of the figure.
cues.evidence: The report’s onset density falls from 3.4 attacks/s at 2:55 to 1.6 at 3:00 and zero at 3:05; relative level reaches −46.5 dB at 3:05. This identifies the closing withdrawal, not an exact release.

transitions.title: The repeated note starts another argument
transitions.how: The first strain closes in D minor; the second takes up the repeated-note idea from that tonal position instead of immediately restoring the opening G minor. The recognisable attack pattern binds the strains together while renewed passagework creates the route back towards the home key.
transitions.evidence: Printed p. 87 ends the first strain with a D-minor cadence and double bar before renewed repeated notes. The report’s strongest boundary is 1:34, following an A-centred span and preceding D-minor estimates; the join is provisionally placed, not bar-aligned.

transitions.title: Repetition gathers into the ending
transitions.how: Near the end, the repeated-note figure passes through different registers while short flourishes expand into descending runs. The final G-minor cadence draws these gestures together. This closing span continues existing material rather than introducing a contrasting tune.
transitions.evidence: Printed p. 89 supplies the alternating registers, runs and G-minor close. The 2:46 measured boundary follows a stronger 2:40–2:45 span; 2:46 labels an approximate closing region, not a single notated cadence.

facts: Organist in French provincial cities, including Clermont-Ferrand; first harpsichord book published in 1706
Traité de l’harmonie, 1722; Nouveau système de musique théorique, 1726
First opera, Hippolyte et Aricie, 1733; tragédies en musique, opéras-ballets and court entertainments
composer.background:
Rameau was born in Dijon, where his father worked as an organist. The documentation of his first four decades is much thinner than that of his Parisian operatic career. He held church appointments in several French cities, published a first book of harpsichord pieces in Paris in 1706, and worked again at Clermont-Ferrand before settling permanently in the capital in the early 1720s. Keyboards, church duties and the analysis of musical practice formed his training. By the time he wrote his first surviving opera he had already published the theoretical book for which his name was known.

The Traité de l’harmonie réduite à ses principes naturels appeared in 1722. Rameau proposed that chords and their connections could be understood through a fundamental bass. Inversion became central: a chord could retain its identity while one of its upper notes moved into the bass. His explanations developed across later books, and his claims to a foundation in nature changed as he engaged with acoustics. The theory attempts to explain why harmonic progressions cohere.
composer.epithet: A theorist of chord roots who began his operatic career at fifty and made harmonic surprise part of French theatrical action.
